headline: Roosevelt signed the internment order, Midway turned the Pacific, and a pile went critical in Chicago
texture: Executive Order 9066 was signed in February and let the army remove people of Japanese descent from the west coast; Canada ordered the same thing. Jimmy Doolittle led a bombing raid on Japan from a carrier deck on April 18. American carriers stopped the Japanese advance at Midway between June 4 and 7. German forces reached Stalingrad on August 23.

Under the bleachers at Stagg Field in Chicago on December 2, the Manhattan Project produced the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction, and the coded message said the Italian navigator had landed in the new world. Nobody outside the project knew any of it had happened.

Bing Crosby's White Christmas was the year's best-selling record, released into the first wartime Christmas with men overseas. Mrs. Miniver took Best Picture and the largest audience of the year, with MGM holding the top two places. Grant Wood died in February, twelve years after painting American Gothic.

notes: Research pass July 2026. The internment order carries a month rather than a day because the source lists it under a month heading. Several claims are general knowledge rather than statements from the year pages: the number interned, Grant Wood painting American Gothic, wartime wages lifting box office and attendance, and war bond appeals in cinema lobbies. Ivande Kaija is described in the source as a Soviet writer, which is how the occupation is recorded there; Latvian is used here because that is what she was.
